conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past seven days; it helps us spot anything we might want to support you with. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the medical team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever is true for you. When you’re ready, we can start with the first question.

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve laughed a little—like when my partner made a silly joke about diaper explosions—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I’m too tired or preoccupied to find things genuinely funny, so I’d say it’s been more difficult than usual.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, I guess. I’ll chuckle if something’s really obvious—like the dog sneaking into the nursery again—but the laughter fades fast and I don’t feel that light, easy feeling I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I still plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s okay—but the excitement isn’t there. Mostly I just hope I’ll have enough energy to get through whatever I’ve planned.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times. Like yesterday when she wouldn’t settle after her feeding and I kept thinking maybe I’m not burping her right or holding her the wrong way. My head knows babies just cry, but I still catch myself wondering what I did to cause it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few nights this week I’ve lain awake with my heart racing, sure something was wrong even though the baby monitor was quiet. I keep checking if she’s breathing, and I replay little things—like whether the diaper rash looked worse—over and over. Nothing huge happened, but the worry just sits there.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but sometimes when she starts to cry I get this sudden knot in my stomach, like I’m afraid I won’t be able to soothe her and something bad will happen. It passes once I pick her up, but those first few seconds feel really tense.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some of the time. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and the instant I think I can shower or close my eyes, the monitor crackles and she’s fussing again. It feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can tick things off, and by dinner I’m just running on fumes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—just keyed-up. I’ll lie there listening for every little grunt, convinced she’s about to wake, and then my mind starts racing about whether I sterilised the bottles properly or packed the diaper-bag right. It takes me ages to drift off, even when the baby’s out cold.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, on and off. There are moments when I look at her little face and feel warm, but then a wave of sadness hits—like I’m mourning the old me, or thinking I’m not cut out for this. It usually lifts if I get a decent stretch of sleep, but it keeps popping up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice when I was really drained and couldn’t get her to latch. My eyes well up, but I blink it away because I’m scared if I start I won’t stop, and she needs me together.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’d never want to leave her or hurt myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed:  
- Marked anhedonia (Q2) and diminished capacity for pleasure/humor (Q1)  
- Frequent, unwarranted self-blame/guilt re infant care (Q3)  
- Persistent, intrusive nocturnal anxiety and somatic tension without identifiable trigger (Q4, Q7)  
- Episodic dread/panic when infant cries, resolving only with direct soothing (Q5)  
- Subjective sadness, tearfulness, and sense of inadequacy "on and off" (Q8, Q9)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and depleted by routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to racing thoughts and hypervigilance about infant safety (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms cluster around low mood, loss of enjoyment, heightened anxiety, and self-doubt about parenting competence.

Screening significance:  
- Meets partial Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) criteria for probable depression and anxiety subscale elevation.  
- No self-harm ideation reported (Q10: denies); therefore no acute safety concern noted at this time.

Risk factors documented:  
- Anhedonia, guilt, sadness, crying episodes, sleep disruption tied to mood, anxiety/panic symptoms, perceived inability to cope.

Summary:  
Client reports several depressive and anxious symptoms that are distressing and functionally impairing in the postpartum period. Results suggest moderate to high likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression and/or anxiety; formal diagnostic evaluation and follow-up care recommended. Safety status stable at screening.
